column1: # Three lines to introduce each region: id<TAB>the land<TAB>the table<TAB>good to know. AI-written from general knowledge, not yet checked by a local.

column2: Misty granite peaks at Huangshan, and villages of white walls and black tile roofs.
column3: Hui cooking is slow-braised, salty and rich, with ham, bamboo shoots and wild mountain greens.
column4: Xuan paper and Hui ink, two classic tools of Chinese calligraphy, both come from here.

column2: A mountainous coast facing Taiwan, with tea hills, round earthen tulou houses and old port cities.
column3: Soups and seafood rule the table, and the oolong teas of Wuyi and Anxi are famous far beyond China.
column4: Many overseas Chinese families trace their roots here, and the local Min speech is very different from Mandarin.

column2: A long corridor of the old Silk Road, from the Yellow River at Lanzhou to the desert caves of Dunhuang.
column3: Hand-pulled beef noodles for breakfast, plenty of lamb, and wheat in every shape.
column4: The Hexi Corridor linked China with Central Asia for two thousand years. The western fort of the Ming Great Wall stands at Jiayuguan.

column2: The busy Pearl River Delta of Guangzhou and Shenzhen, backed by green hills and a long coast.
column3: Cantonese cooking prizes freshness: dim sum, roast goose, steamed fish and slow-simmered soups.
column4: Cantonese (粤语) is the everyday language, and this has been China's southern door to the world for centuries.

column2: Karst peaks rising straight out of rivers and rice fields around Guilin and Yangshuo.
column3: Rice noodles everywhere, from gentle Guilin noodles to Liuzhou's pungent snail noodles, with sour and spicy flavors.
column4: This is the home region of the Zhuang, China's largest minority people, who are known for their folk songs.

column2: Green mountains, waterfalls and caves, in one of the most rugged corners of China.
column3: Sour and spicy at once: sour-soup fish, chili in almost everything, and Moutai liquor.
column4: Miao and Dong villages fill the hills, with silver jewelry, wooden drum towers and songs in many voices.

column2: China's tropical island: palm beaches, rainforest mountains and warm winters.
column3: Light and fresh food, with Wenchang chicken, coconut, seafood and tropical fruit.
column4: The Li people have lived here for thousands of years. Today the island is China's favorite winter escape.

column2: The plain around the capital, with the Great Wall running over the hills. This trip also takes in Beijing and Tianjin.
column3: Northern wheat food: dumplings, noodles and flatbreads, and of course Peking duck in Beijing.
column4: Standard Mandarin is based on the speech of Beijing, so this is where your textbook Chinese sounds most at home.

column2: China's far northeast: long frozen winters, deep forests and the Russian border along the Amur River.
column3: Hearty stews, dumplings and sweet-and-sour pork, plus Russian-style bread and sausage in Harbin.
column4: Every winter Harbin builds a whole park of buildings from blocks of ice and lights them from inside.

column2: The Central Plains along the Yellow River, a cradle of Chinese civilization with several ancient capitals.
column3: Noodles and soups: braised hui mian, and peppery hulatang soup for breakfast.
column4: Shaolin Temple, the home of kung fu, is here, and so are the oracle bones of Anyang, the oldest Chinese writing.

column2: Towers packed between green peaks and a famous harbor, with quiet islands and beaches a ferry ride away.
column3: Dim sum, roast meats, milk tea and cha chaan teng diners, where East and West share one table.
column4: Cantonese and English are the main languages, and writing uses traditional characters.

column2: The middle Yangtze: lakes, the Three Gorges and the big river city of Wuhan.
column3: Hot dry noodles for breakfast, freshwater fish, and lotus root soup.
column4: Wudang Mountain is a center of Taoism and tai chi, and the Three Gorges Dam is the largest power station in the world.

column2: Rice fields, Dongting Lake and the sandstone pillars of Zhangjiajie.
column3: Xiang cooking is fiery and sour, with chopped chilies, smoked pork and stinky tofu.
column4: A popular saying goes that people here are only afraid of food that is not spicy. Mao Zedong was born in this province.

column2: Canals, gardens and water towns on the lower Yangtze. This trip also takes in Shanghai.
column3: Delicate and a little sweet: soup dumplings, salted duck, hairy crab and Yangzhou fried rice.
column4: The classical gardens of Suzhou and kunqu opera are both recognized by UNESCO.

column2: Green hills around Poyang Lake, the largest freshwater lake in China, with the mountains Lushan and Sanqingshan.
column3: Spicy home cooking, rice noodles and soups simmered in clay jars.
column4: Jingdezhen has made porcelain for more than a thousand years and is called the porcelain capital.

column2: Forests, snow, and the volcanic crater lake on Changbai Mountain at the North Korean border.
column3: Northeastern stews beside Korean flavors: cold noodles, kimchi and barbecue.
column4: Many ethnic Koreans live in Yanbian, where street signs are written in both Korean and Chinese.

column2: The southern gate of the northeast, with the old Manchu capital Shenyang and the seaside city of Dalian.
column3: Dumplings, barbecue and stews inland, and seafood on the coast.
column4: The Qing dynasty began here before it moved to Beijing, and Shenyang still has its own imperial palace.

column2: A tiny peninsula and two islands across the Pearl River from Hong Kong, with pastel Portuguese squares and giant casinos.
column3: Macanese food mixes Portuguese and Cantonese cooking: egg tarts, pork chop buns and African chicken.
column4: Portugal ran Macau until 1999. Cantonese is the daily language, and Portuguese is still an official one.

column2: A wide arc of grassland, desert and forest along China's northern border.
column3: Lamb, salty milk tea, dried cheese and oat noodles.
column4: Mongolian is still written here in its traditional top-to-bottom script, and Naadam festivals bring wrestling, archery and horse racing.

column2: A small region where the Yellow River waters green fields between the desert and the Helan Mountains.
column3: Hand-grabbed lamb, eight-treasure tea and goji berries.
column4: Many Hui Muslims live here, and this was once the heart of the Western Xia kingdom.

column2: High plateau and salt lakes, and the place where the Yellow River, the Yangtze and the Mekong all begin.
column3: Yak meat, yogurt, barley and hand-pulled noodles.
column4: Tibetan, Hui, Tu and Mongol cultures meet here, around the largest lake in China.

column2: Loess hills in the north, the Qinling mountains in the south, and the old capital Xi'an on the plain between.
column3: Wheat country: roujiamo, belt-wide biangbiang noodles, and lamb soup with crumbled bread.
column4: Xi'an, once called Chang'an, was the capital of more than ten dynasties, among them the Han and the Tang.

column2: A peninsula between the Bohai and Yellow seas, with sacred Mount Tai and the coast city of Qingdao.
column3: Lu cooking is one of China's great traditions: seafood, scallions and big steamed buns, washed down with Tsingtao beer.
column4: Confucius was born in Qufu, where his temple and his family's mansion still stand.

column2: A plateau of loess hills west of the Taihang Mountains, full of old temples and walled towns.
column3: Noodles in countless shapes, always with a splash of aged vinegar.
column4: Shanxi keeps a great share of China's oldest wooden buildings, and its merchants ran early banks from Pingyao.

column2: A warm, misty basin ringed by mountains, with the Tibetan highlands to the west. This trip also takes in Chongqing.
column3: Málà (麻辣): chili heat plus the numbing tingle of Sichuan pepper, from mapo tofu to hot pot.
column4: Giant pandas live in the bamboo forests here, and Chengdu is famous for its teahouses and its easy pace.

column2: An island city-state at the tip of the Malay Peninsula, green, hot and humid all year.
column3: Hawker centers serve Chinese, Malay and Indian dishes side by side: chicken rice, laksa and satay.
column4: Mandarin is one of four official languages, with English, Malay and Tamil, and it is written in simplified characters.

column2: A mountainous island of high peaks, hot springs, east-coast cliffs and busy western cities.
column3: Night markets, beef noodles, bubble tea and endless small eats (小吃).
column4: Mandarin here is written in traditional characters, and children learn to read with Zhuyin symbols, not pinyin.

column2: China's largest region: deserts and oases, split in two by the snowy Tianshan range.
column3: Lamb skewers, naan, pilaf and hand-pulled noodles, with very sweet melons and grapes.
column4: Uyghur, Kazakh and many other cultures live along the old Silk Road routes here.

column2: The roof of the world: a plateau more than 4,000 meters high, with the Himalayas along its southern edge.
column3: Butter tea, tsampa (roasted barley flour) and yak.
column4: Tibetan Buddhism shapes daily life here, from prayer flags on the passes to pilgrims walking around temples.

column2: Snow mountains near Tibet at one end and tropical forest near Laos and Myanmar at the other. Kunming is called the Spring City.
column3: Rice noodles, wild mushrooms, edible flowers, local cheese and Pu'er tea.
column4: Twenty-five of China's minority peoples live in Yunnan, more than in any other province.

column2: Hills, tea fields and water towns south of Shanghai, with West Lake at Hangzhou and many islands offshore.
column3: Fresh and light: lake fish, Dongpo pork, Longjing tea and Shaoxing rice wine.
column4: Hangzhou was the capital of the Southern Song dynasty, and today the province is a center of online trade.
